newsitem.title: INDIA: India's leading parties face trouble within.
newsitem.headline: India's leading parties face trouble within.

text.p: Two of Indias leading political parties, locked in an uneasy relationship, were grappling on Sunday with internal troubles ahead of party elections later this month.
The Congress party, Indias oldest political machine, is scheduled to elect a president on June 9. One day later, Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujrals Janata Dal will do the same.

Leadership challengers in both parties say their current heads cannot deliver the goods in mid-term polls, seen inevitable by many because the fragmented parliament has seen much turmoil since April/May 1996 general elections.

Both parties are struggling under orders from the independent Election Commission, which has forced them to follow their party constitutions, long buried under the rubble of overwhelming personality politics.
The commissions order came at a time when the leaders of both parties were facing a serious crisis of reputation.
With the electoral process under way, the incumbent leaders are seen by party rivals as blocking smooth internal polls.

In the Congress party, which has ruled India for all but five years since independence in 1947, Rajesh Pilot and Sharad Pawar, two relatively young leaders, have mounted an attack on incumbent president Sitaram Kesri, 76.
Pawar and Pilot accuse Kesri of manipulating the election of around 8,000 district-level delegates who will vote for a president.
Analysts say Kesri has enough support from four key states to see him through the challenge.

(The) Congress party has a tradition of unity and also of rallying around the leader. The structure of the electoral college helps him (Kesri), political analyst Mahesh Rangarajan of the Centre for Contemporary Studies told Reuters.

Kesri, whose party offers vital support to the Janata Dal-led United Front government, in April toppled the coalition government headed by then prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda and renewed support only after the front changed its leader.
The two groups had closed ranks last year to keep from power the Hindu nationalists, who hold the most seats in parliament.
Rivals say Kesri cannot bring victory to a party hit by corruption scandals and losing its traditional support from low castes and Moslem minority voters.
The result is a call for change, apparently inspired in part by the victory in May of Tony Blairs Labour Party in Britain.
All over the world, young leaders are stepping forward to take over the mantle, and if I am not that young, I am also not that old, Pawar, 56, told the Sunday Observer.
Weeks after Kesri's was hit by political troubles, federal police decided to prosecute Janata Dal president Laloo Prasad Yadav in a $280-million fodder scandal.

Yadav, who denies any wrongdoing, faces charges of being a party to divert animal welfare funds in the eastern state of Bihar, of which he is chief minister. He has so far refused to resign from office and face trial.
Laloo is being challenged by Sharad Yadav, a fellow low-caste leader who lacks his presidents mass appeal.
Janata Dal seems to be in serious trouble because he (Laloo) is the only leader with a mass base, Rangarajan said. This is going to be crucial for the survival of the government (of Gujral).
But the challenger is said to have strong support among delegates who will choose the new party head. Dont be surprised if Sharad Yadav pulls a surprise, Rangarajan said.
